turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Well, to be honest, it’s just been so incredibly frustrating lately, and I really didn't want to come in, but... gosh, I just don't know what else to do. I’ve been working as an administrative assistant for years, basically right out of high school, so my whole life is supposed to be about keeping track of details, you know? I'm supposed to be the one who organizes things and keeps everything running smoothly. 

But what finally made me actually pick up the phone and ask for help—and honestly, it took me weeks to even make this appointment—is that I just keep forgetting these little things that I normally handle without a second thought. It's driving me crazy. Like, I’ll completely forget to return phone calls, which is literally part of my job. Or I'll have a simple registration form that I just need to sign and turn in, and I'll leave it sitting right there on the kitchen counter for days and just... totally blank on actually taking it with me. 

And it’s happening with my personal errands, too. I can't tell you how many times lately I’ve told myself, "Okay, you absolutely have to stop at the store on the way home," and then I’ll just drive straight home on autopilot. I'll literally pull into my driveway, put the car in park, and then realize I completely forgot to stop for the errand. It’s just these little daily things, but it’s happening so much and it's so unlike how I usually am, that I just felt like I had to talk to someone about it before I end up getting in trouble at work or something.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly reports frequently forgetting daily activities and tasks, such as returning phone calls, bringing forms with them, and running errands on the way home.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first start noticing these memory and attention problems? Did they come on suddenly over days or weeks, or have they been gradually getting worse over months?

It's been more of a slow build, but I can actually pinpoint when it started to become a real, noticeable issue for me. 

It was about 15 months ago. I remember because that's when I decided to go back to school—well, not a full degree, but an evening certificate program to maybe help me move up at work. I was so excited about it. I bought all these new notebooks and highlighters, and I had this whole color-coded system planned out for my schedule between work and classes. But almost as soon as the program started, it was like my brain just couldn't hold all the pieces together anymore. I thought, "Okay, this is just an adjustment period," but it never really got better. The attention issues, the struggling to keep things organized... it all just became noticeably harder to manage right around that 15-month mark when I added the evening classes to my plate. And it's just been this constant, exhausting effort ever since then to try and keep my head above water with everything.

So physically putting things where they belong, or figuring out how to fit boxes into the supply closet so everything fits perfectly, I'm great at that. I have a really good eye for it. It's just... it's just remembering to actually *do* the tasks that's the problem, not the physical space or time or my words. So physically, my body feels totally normal. No weird aches, no changes in my appetite—I still love those blueberry scones a little too much!—no feeling weak or sick. turns.doctor_question: When you forget to do these tasks at work or forget to run errands, do you find yourself feeling guilty or blaming yourself harshly, or does it feel more like just frustration with the situation itself?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely just frustration. I mean, I don't... I don't sit there and think I'm a horrible person or anything like that. It's not this deep, heavy guilt where I feel like a failure at life. It's really just pure, unadulterated annoyance with myself. 

Like, okay, for example, just last Tuesday at work. I'm a secretary, so keeping the office running smoothly is literally my entire job description, right? Well, we have this massive copier down the hall—it's one of those huge industrial ones that does the stapling and the hole punching and the sorting, but it takes this very specific, incredibly expensive toner that we have to special order. My boss asked me to order a backup cartridge on Monday morning because we were getting low. Well, Tuesday afternoon rolls around, the 'replace toner' light starts flashing red, and it just hit me like a ton of bricks. I completely forgot to place the order. 

But when that happened, I didn't go into a spiral about it. I didn't feel worthless or hate myself. I was just really, really irritated. I literally slapped my forehead and went, "Ugh, seriously? Come on, you knew you had to do this!" I just felt silly. And then I had to scramble and call the supplier and beg them to overnight it, which they did, thank goodness, but it was just an unnecessary headache, you know? 

And it's the exact same thing with personal errands. Like, last week I needed to pick up my winter coat from the dry cleaners. It's this little place right on my way home from work, I literally drive past it every single day. I told myself all day, "Don't forget the coat, don't forget the coat." And what did I do? I drove right past it, pulled into my driveway, turned off the car, and realized my back seat was empty. I didn't cry or feel guilty, I just let out this huge groan and gripped the steering wheel like, "Why are you like this?!" 

So, yeah, it's not guilt. I know I'm a good person, and I know I'm a hard worker. I just get so incredibly frustrated that I can't seem to keep all the plates spinning right now without dropping one, especially when it's something so simple. I just wish I didn't have to constantly leave myself a million sticky notes—which half the time fall off my computer monitor anyway—just to remember basic things! But no, no harsh self-blame or anything dark like that. Just annoyance.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting down trying to focus on one specific task—like reading an email from your boss or working through a problem at work—can you actually concentrate and pay attention to that one thing, or do you find your mind wandering or jumping around even when you're really trying to focus?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, my mind definitely jumps around. It is so hard to just lock in on one thing, no matter how hard I try. Like, okay, our office setup is probably part of the problem, I think, because my desk is right out in the open since I'm the first point of contact. But honestly, whether I'm at the office or, gosh, even when I was taking that evening continuing education class for QuickBooks a few months ago, it’s the exact same story. 

I will be sitting there, staring right at an email from my boss—and he writes these incredibly dense, multi-paragraph emails that you really can't skim, you have to read every single word—and I'll be trying so, so hard to focus on it. But then, just one phone ringing is all it takes. And it doesn't even have to be my phone! It could be Dave's phone all the way across the room, but the second it rings, my attention is just completely hijacked. I'll look up, I'll wonder who's calling him, I'll wonder if it's that difficult client we had last week... 

Or if there are people talking nearby... oh, forget about it. If Jessica and Tom are standing by the printer chatting about their weekend plans, I literally cannot tune them out. I’ll be looking at my computer monitor, nodding to myself like I'm reading, but my brain is one hundred percent focused on Tom’s story about his dog. 

And the funny thing is, it doesn't even have to be an actual, physical distraction in the room! Sometimes it’s just my own brain. I could be in a totally quiet space, right in the middle of working through a scheduling problem, and suddenly a random thought about something at home will just pop into my head out of nowhere. I'll be typing away and suddenly think, "Wait, did I remember to take the chicken out of the freezer?" or "I really need to measure that space in the hallway to see if a new shoe rack will fit." And just like that, I am completely pulled off what I was working on. I'll end up staring into space for five minutes before I realize I haven't read a single word of that email. It’s like my brain is a television and someone else has the remote, just constantly changing the channel on me when I’m trying to watch one specific show. So, yes, even when I am really, really trying to concentrate, I just get derailed so easily by almost anything.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back to when you were in elementary school or middle school, before you started this job as an administrative assistant—do you remember having similar kinds of trouble back then? Like, did your teachers ever mention that you had difficulty paying attention in class, or did you find yourself fidgeting a lot even as a kid?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, wow, yes. Going all the way back to elementary school, it was... well, it was a whole ordeal, honestly. My mom and I actually joke about it now, but back then it was incredibly frustrating for her. I don't know if my teachers specifically used the word fidgeting on my report cards, but they definitely noticed I was struggling to keep things together and stay on track. 

I was absolutely that kid who lost her homework in her backpack. I had this bright purple Lisa Frank backpack—the one with the neon dolphins, I loved that thing so much—but the inside of it was just a complete disaster zone. It was like a black hole. I would do my math worksheet at the kitchen table, put it in my folder, put the folder in the backpack, and then somehow by nine in the morning the next day, it was just gone. The teacher would ask for it, and I’d be digging through old wrappers, broken crayons, and just mounds of crumpled paper at the bottom of the bag, and I just couldn't find it. 

And permission slips! Oh my gosh, forget about it. I was notorious for forgetting permission slips. We would have these field trips, like I remember this one specific trip to the natural history museum in third grade, and the teacher had handed out the bright yellow slips a week in advance. I stuffed it in my desk, or my bag, and completely forgot it existed until the morning we were supposed to get on the bus. My mom actually had to leave her job, drive all the way to the school, and sign a spare copy in the front office so I wouldn't have to stay behind in the library. She would always find the original slip like three weeks later, completely crinkled up under a squished juice box.

It was the exact same story with any kind of assignment, too. If we had a project, I just couldn't stay focused on it. I needed my mother, or my teacher—like Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, she was such a saint—they literally had to remind me step by step to finish projects. If they just told me to build a diorama by Friday, I would stare at the shoebox and get completely overwhelmed or distracted by the glue sticks. My mom would have to sit right next to me and tell me to paint the background first, and then tell me to wait for it to dry, and then remind me to cut out the trees. If she didn't walk me through it and constantly remind me of the very next step, I would just wander off or start playing with the modeling clay and completely forget what I was supposed to be doing. So, yeah, this definitely isn't a new thing for me, it's been happening since I was little.
